text:
Weeks and months pass again, and spring came. The snow was already gone; far out in space there was a roaring as of waters released from the sun to the moon. The swallows had come, and in the forest outside the town a lively life awoke, of all kinds of leaping animals and birds with foreign tongues. A fresh, sweetish smell drifted up from the earth.

His work has lasted the whole winter. Like a work song, the poplars’ dry branches had creaked against the wall of the house night and day; now spring had come, the storms were past, and the stamping mill had creaked to a halt.

He opens the window and looks out; the street is already quiet although it is not midnight, the stars twinkle in a cloudless sky, and tomorrow promises to be a warm and bright day. He hears the rumble from the town mingling with the eternal roar in the distance. Suddenly a railway whistle shrills; it is the night train’s signal; it sounds like a single cockcrow in the still night. Now the time for work has come; this train whistle has been like a summons to him all winter.

And he closes the window and sits down at the table again. He throws aside the books he has been reading and brings out the papers. He takes up the pen.

Now his great work is almost finished; it lacks only a final chapter, a greeting as though from a ship sailing away, and he already has it in his head:

A gentleman is sitting in an inn by the road; he is passing through and is going far, far out into the world. His hair and beard are gray, and many years have passed over him; but he is still big and strong, and he is hardly as old as he looks. Outside stands his carriage, the horses are resting, the coachman is happy and content; for the stranger has given him wine and food. When the gentleman has entered his name, the innkeeper recognizes him and bows to him and shows him great honor. Who lives at the Castle now? the gentleman asks. The innkeeper answers: The Captain; he is very rich; his wife is good to everyone. To everyone? the gentleman asks himself and smiles strangely, to me as well? And the gentleman sits down to write on a piece of paper, and when it is filled he reads it over; it is a poem, grave and calm, but with many bitter words. But afterward he tears the paper to pieces, and he continues to sit there and tear the paper into still smaller pieces. Then there is a knock at his door, and a woman clad in yellow enters. She lifts her veil; it is the lady of the Castle, Mrs. Victoria. She is like a majesty. The gentleman rises abruptly; his dark soul is as though lit by a flash of lightning at that very moment. You are so good to everyone, he says bitterly; You come to me as well. She does not answer; she merely stands and looks at him, and her face turns a dusky red. What do You want? he asks, just as bitterly as before: have You come to remind me of what is past? For then it is for the last time, gracious lady; now I am leaving forever. And still the young lady of the Castle does not answer, but her mouth trembles. He says: Is it not enough for You that I have acknowledged my folly once? Then hear me, I do so again: my heart was set on You, I was not worthy of You—are You satisfied now? He continues with mounting vehemence: You answered me no, You took another; I was a peasant, a bear, a barbarian who in his youth had blundered into a royal game preserve! But then the gentleman throws himself onto a chair and sobs and begs: Oh, go! Forgive me, go Your way! Now all the flush has left the lady of the Castle’s face. Then she says, pronouncing the words so slowly and distinctly: I love You; misunderstand me no longer, it is You whom I love; farewell! And the young lady of the Castle turned away; she put her hands over her face and went quickly out of the door....

He puts down the pen and leans back. Yes, full stop, the end. There lay the book, all the written pages, nine months’ work. A warm satisfaction ripples through him because his work has been brought to completion. And while he sits there looking toward the window through which day is dawning, it hums and pounds in his head, and his spirit continues to work. He is full of feeling; his brain lies like an unharvested wild garden from whose earth steam rises:

In some mysterious way he has entered a deep, extinct valley where no living thing is to be found. Far away, alone and forgotten, an organ stands playing. He goes nearer to it, he examines it; the organ is bleeding, blood runs from one of its sides while it plays. Farther on he comes to a square. Everything there is deserted; no tree can be seen and no sound can be heard; it is merely an empty square. But in the sand are marks left by people’s shoes, and the last words spoken in the place seem still to remain in the air, so recently was it abandoned. A strange sensation fills him; these words remaining in the air above the square distress him, come nearer to him, press upon him. He strikes them away from himself and they return; they are not words, they are old men, a group of old men dancing; he sees them now. Why are they dancing, and why are they not in the least happy when they dance? A cold, ghastly air emanates from this company of old men; they do not see him, they are blind, and when he calls to them they do not hear him, they are dead. He wanders toward the east, toward the sun; he comes to a mountain. A voice calls: Are you beside a mountain? Yes, he answers, I am standing beside a mountain. Then the voice says: The mountain beside which you stand is my foot; I lie bound in the outermost land; come and free me!

Then he sets out for the outermost land. By a bridge a man stands lying in wait for him; he collects shadows; the man is made of musk. An icy terror grips him at the sight of this man who means to take his shadow. He spits at him and threatens him with clenched fists, but the man stands motionless and waits for him. Turn back! a voice calls behind him. He turns and sees a head rolling along the road and showing him the direction. The head is a human head, and now and then it laughs softly and soundlessly. He follows it. It rolls for days and nights, and he follows it; at the seashore it slips down into the earth and hides. He wades out into the sea and dives. He stands before a mighty gate and encounters a large, barking fish. It has a mane on its neck and barks at him like a dog. Behind the fish stands Victoria. He stretches his hands out toward her; she has no clothes on, she laughs toward him, and a storm blows through her hair. Then he calls out to her, he himself hears his scream—and wakes.

Johannes rises and goes to the window. It has grown almost light, and in the little mirror on the window jamb he sees that his temples are red. He puts out the lamp and, once more, in the gray light of day, reads the last page of his book. Then he lies down.

By the afternoon of that same day Johannes had paid for his room, delivered his manuscript, and left the town. He had gone abroad; no one knew where.
